doc.title: Jon-Erik Kellso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Tom Saunders, Wild Bill Davison, Doc Cheatham and J.C. Heard's concert
summary: He met Wild Bill Davison via Tom Saunders, played in New McKinney's Cottonpickers with Doc Cheatham, and in J.C. Heard's band at a concert where Heard died the night before and Dizzy Gillespie paid tribute.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans

blocks.x: Have you been able to kind of play alongside some of your influences or heroes?

Yeah. That’s a good one. Yeah, I was very fortunate. Aside from meeting the local heroes around Detroit and playing with some of them, which were probably mostly names you might not know but it was a thrill, every year I’d get to play with better and better musicians. One of the first ones I got to play with was a guy named Tom Saunders in Detroit, who is a very great cornet player and I used to go and hear him when I wasn’t even really old enough to be in the bars that he was playing in, but we’d go and hear him, and he introduced me to Wild Bill Davison. He was sort of a protege friend of Wild Bill’s. And he used to bring in Wild Bill to this club that he played in in the Detroit area whenever he could. And sometimes he’d have him in town for a week or two weeks or something like that, or just one concert. And so he put on a concert called “Four Generations of Jazz Cornet” and I was the young generation, there was a guy from Boston named Paul Monnet, who was maybe in his thirties at the time, and then Tom was in his forties, maybe fifties at the time, and then Wild Bill, I don’t remember how old he was at the time, you know, pushing 80 I suppose, I’m not sure. But that was when I was about 17 or 18 I think when we did that. So that was a thrill. I got to meet Wild Bill who was one of my favorites at the time and still is. And I got to play with Doc Cheatham a couple of times, and that was exciting. We had a group in Detroit called “The New McKinney’s Cottonpickers” which was based on the original McKinney’s Cottonpickers, which was a Detroit group, way, way, way back, which had included Doc Cheatham and Benny Carter and all kinds of great players. And so we put on this concert, this was one of the greatest days of my life. It was at Detroit’s Orchestra Hall, which some say the acoustics are better than Carnegie Hall. And I was playing in two different groups that were the two featured groups on this concert. So it was “The New McKinney’s Cottonpickers” featuring Doc Cheatham, which was a thrill. And then I was in this group, J.C. Heard’s Big Band, and of course J.C. Heard was one of the great jazz drummers and he settled in Detroit and had a very good big band that I played with. And he and Dizzy Gillespie shared the same birthday, same year, and they were friends from way, way back, and so the idea was to have the two of them celebrate their birthday together in this concert. And this was the other half of this concert. I got to meet and play with two of my all-time idols. So the sad part of it was J.C. Heard passed away the night before the

concert, which was a shock. He was going to be 72 I believe. We had played with him two nights before, and he was in great shape and full of energy and playing great, no signs of any health problems. He just all of a sudden had a heart attack and that was it. And I’ll never forget how well Dizzy Gillespie handled this. We did the concert with one of J.C.’s proteges, a guy named Billy Cairo, a drummer in Detroit, and Dizzy managed to pay tribute to J.C., his old friend, really nicely, but also make it a happy thing and remember the good times and tell some funny stories and just made people feel good, you know, instead of it being like this whole downer. So that was a real exciting thing for me.
He certainly had that knack of making people feel good.
